source_text: Ergo non ad scripturas provocandum est, nec in his constituendum certamen in quibus aut nulla aut incerta victoria est aut parum certa. Nam etsi non ita evaderet conlatio scripturarum, ut utramque partem parem sisteret, ordo rerum desiderabat illud prius proponi, quod nunc solum disputandum est: quibus competat fides ipsa, cuius sint scripturae, a quo, et per quos, et quando, et quibus sit tradita disciplina qua fiunt Christiani. Ubi enim apparuerit esse veritatem disciplinae et fidei Christianae, illic erit veritas scripturarum et expositionum et omnium traditionum Christianarum.
thought_title: The contest must first be over who owns the faith
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that heretics have no right to debate Scripture, because the prior question is who the Scriptures and the faith belong to.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore one must not appeal to the Scriptures, nor must a contest be established in these things in which either there is no victory or the victory is uncertain or too little certain. For even if the comparison of the Scriptures did not turn out in such a way that it made each side stand equal, the order of things was requiring that that be proposed first, which alone must now be disputed: to whom the faith itself belongs, whose the Scriptures are, from whom, and through whom, and when, and to whom the discipline by which people become Christians was handed down. For where it will have appeared that the truth of the discipline and of the Christian faith is, there will be the truth of the Scriptures and of the expositions and of all the Christian traditions.

choices.english: one must not appeal to the Scriptures
choices.why: The impersonal gerundive keeps the legal tone of a procedural rule; 'appeal' matches the forensic context of praescriptio.
rejected: there must be no appeal to the Scriptures
the Scriptures must not be appealed to

choices.english: nor must a contest be established in these things
choices.why: Keeps the parallel impersonal gerundive construction and the forensic sense of certamen as a formal dispute.
rejected: nor should a struggle be set up in them
nor is a battle to be joined in these

choices.english: the order of things was requiring
choices.why: Desidero here has the sense of logical necessity, not mere wishing; 'order of things' preserves the procedural sequence Tertullian insists on.

choices.english: to whom the faith itself belongs
choices.why: Competo in legal Latin means 'belong to, be the property of'; this is the core ownership question Tertullian raises.
rejected: to whom the faith is suited
for whom the faith is fitting

choices.english: the discipline by which people become Christians
choices.why: Fiunt is passive of facio, 'are made'; the impersonal 'people' avoids adding a subject not in the Latin while keeping the sense of becoming.
rejected: the discipline by which Christians are made
the teaching through which they become Christians

choices.english: there will be the truth of the Scriptures
choices.why: Illíc is emphatic and spatial, pointing to the church where the faith is; the future tense is preserved.
rejected: in that place will be the truth of the Scriptures
there the truth of the Scriptures will be

pass_b_english: So there must be no appeal to the Scriptures, and no contest established in them where victory is either nonexistent, or uncertain, or not certain enough. For even if a comparison of the Scriptures did not turn out in such a way as to make both sides stand equal, the order of things was requiring that this be proposed first, which alone is now to be disputed: to whom the faith itself belongs, whose the Scriptures are, from whom, and through whom, and when, and to whom was handed down the discipline by which people become Christians. For where it has appeared that the truth of the Christian discipline and faith is, there will be the truth of the Scriptures and of their interpretations and of all Christian traditions.

last_rejected.quote: to whom was handed down the discipline by which people become Christians
last_rejected.source_quote: et quibus sit tradita disciplina qua fiunt Christiani
last_rejected.why: Latin asks who handed down the discipline (agents), but English makes the recipients the focus, reversing agency.
last_rejected.fix: by whom the discipline by which Christians are made was handed down
last_rejected.ruling: quibus is dative; tradita disciplina goes 'to whom' (recipients). English correctly renders recipients, not agents.
